name: Cream crackle marble (Crema Marfil Coto, Pinoso, Alicante)
summary: A cream, compact nummulitic limestone sold as marble, crossed by a network of fine veins and stylolites that reads as a crackle; laid down on the sea floor about 50 million years ago and quarried on Monte El Coto at Pinoso (Alicante, Spain). It is the Rotunda's marble: its walls, its pilasters and the sun clock's drum, honed, and glass-smooth where the future rooms carry it on.

class.text: A nummulitic limestone, petrographically a biosparite(-biomicrite) with veins and stylolites; a commercial marble (it meets the Marble Institute of America's requirements), not a metamorphic one.

chosenBecause.text: Its veins form a network rather than parallel lines: five families of discontinuity planes cross it (open stylolites, partly open stylolites, stylolites cemented with iron oxides and clay minerals, stylolites cemented with calcite, and calcite veins).

chosenBecause.text: It is cream-coloured with 'refined tones and discrete natural veins': a biosparite of foraminifera with irregularly distributed calcite veins.
chosenBecause.source: Levantina, 'Crema Marfil Coto: ficha tecnica / technical file' (UNE-EN and ASTM test results), pp. 1-4, https://www.levantina.com/files/3351814979b33856c831796bdbd7340f/10004220/1/cremamarfil-2.pdf

chosenBecause.text: The one local photograph of a cream compact stone, Poly Haven marble_01 ('smooth, even cream-beige tiles with subtle veining and low sheen'), shows a fine dark vein network on a cream ground (see evidence).

alternativesConsidered.designation: Botticino Classico (Botticino, Rezzato and Mazzano, east of Brescia, Italy)
alternativesConsidered.reason: The classical Italian cream 'marble': a compact, partly dolomitised micritic limestone of the Corna Formation (Jurassic), white through ivory with hints of chestnut. Set aside as the crackle because its stylolites are thin, chestnut-coloured and run almost parallel to the bedding, so its veining reads as lines, not as a network.

formation.how: Shells of foraminifera (nummulites) and lime mud gathered on the sea floor in the early Eocene and were cemented into a biosparite. The rock was later cut by stylolites, jagged seams lined with iron oxides and clay, and by fractures healed with white calcite; together they make the crackle.

specularF0.conditions: normal incidence from air, 589.3 nm (0.0536 at 550 nm)
specularF0.derivation: F = ((n - 1) / (n + 1))^2. A face cut through randomly oriented calcite grains: half the light meets n_o (F = 0.0613); half meets n_e(theta), with 1/n_e(theta)^2 = cos^2(theta)/n_o^2 + sin^2(theta)/n_e^2, averaged over the sphere of grain orientations (mean F = 0.0453); 0.5 x 0.0613 + 0.5 x 0.0453 = 0.0533. min is F(n_e) and max is F(n_o), the extremes a single grain shows.

wet.text: A wet face darkens: water in the pores and on the surface lowers the index step at the grains, and the water film traps diffusely reflected light by total internal reflection, so more of it is absorbed.

photograph: A cream ground, even in tone, crossed by fine jagged seams in several directions that join into a network of irregular cells.
The darker seams (stylolites with iron oxides and clay) are grey-brown and toothed; the paler ones (calcite) are white and smoother.
Some slabs carry small fossil grains, white coin-sized spots or wavy figures; grades differ by vein density.
Honed: a low, even sheen, the veins soft. Polished: a deep gloss in which the veins sharpen and the ground warms.
Thin pieces break along the seams: look for resin-mended cracks that follow a vein.
